chapter_name: Sangya Aur Uske Bhed (Nouns and Their Types)
learning_objective: 🎯 By the end of this chapter, you will master the naming words of the universe and learn how to categorize absolutely everything around you!

main_concepts.concept_title: 🏷️ What is Sangya? (The Universal Name Tag)
main_concepts.simple_explanation: Imagine a world where nothing has a name. You wouldn't be able to ask for an 'apple' or call your 'friend'! 'Sangya' is simply a name tag. The name of any person, place, animal, thing, or even an invisible feeling is called a Noun.

If I say 'Boy' (लड़का), it could be anyone—this is Jativachak (Common Noun). But if I say 'Virat Kohli', that is a specific VIP person—this is Vyaktivachak (Proper Noun). 'City' is Common, 'Delhi' is Proper!

Can you touch 'Honesty' (ईमानदारी)? Can you put 'Childhood' (बचपन) in a box? No! Bhavavachak Sangyas are the names of feelings, qualities, or states of being. You can only feel or experience them, not physically touch them.

These are nouns for things we weigh or measure but cannot count directly. Think of raw materials and liquids like Gold (सोना), Water (पानी), Wood (लकड़ी), or Rice (चावल). You say 'give me some water', not 'give me one water'!

When a single word represents a whole group or team of things, it is a Collective Noun. Examples include Army (सेना), Class (कक्षा), Crowd (भीड़), or a Bunch of keys (गुच्छा). It sounds singular, but it packs a crowd inside!

fun_activity.title: 📝 The 'Name, Place, Animal, Thing' Master
fun_activity.instructions: Pick a letter (e.g., 'M' / 'म'). Quickly write down a Vyaktivachak Sangya (Person/Place), a Jativachak Sangya (Animal/Thing), and a Bhavavachak Sangya (Feeling/Quality) starting with that letter! Time yourself for 30 seconds.

quick_recap: ⭐ Sangya is the name of any person, place, thing, or emotion.
⭐ Vyaktivachak (Proper Noun) points to specific names; Jativachak (Common Noun) points to general categories.
⭐ Bhavavachak (Abstract Noun) names feelings, ideas, and states that cannot be physically touched.
⭐ Dravyavachak refers to materials and liquids, while Samuhavachak refers to groups or collections.
